items.headline: Give Your AI Coding Agent a rules.md File
items.background: Developers using AI coding agents like Cursor or Copilot frequently find themselves repeating the same constraints and context in every session — 'don't touch this file,' 'use this pattern,' etc. There's no built-in memory across sessions in most tools.
keyFindings: A rules.md file gives the AI persistent project-level context it can reference across sessions, reducing repeated corrections.
The file can specify coding conventions, off-limits files, preferred libraries, and architectural decisions the AI should respect.
This approach works across multiple AI coding tools that support system-level or project-level instruction files.
items.implications: If your team uses AI coding assistants, a shared rules.md in the repo root is a low-effort way to enforce consistency and reduce AI-generated drift from your codebase conventions. Especially useful when multiple team members use different AI tools on the same project.

items.headline: AI Won't Replace Designers — It Exposes Weak Process
items.background: The 'will AI replace designers?' debate has been running for years, often generating more anxiety than insight. This piece shifts the framing away from job replacement toward what AI actually threatens.
keyFindings: AI tools are absorbing tasks that designers used to use as proxies for skill — wireframing speed, asset generation, copy iteration — making pure execution less defensible as a value proposition.
The argument is that designers who relied on tool proficiency over strategic thinking are most exposed.
Designers who can define problems, conduct research, and make defensible decisions remain difficult to automate.
items.implications: Worth reading as a prompt to audit your own practice: if most of your documented value is in deliverable production rather than decision-making, that's the real risk to address. Not an immediate threat assessment but a useful reframing for career positioning.

items.headline: Good Interfaces Move Users Forward, Not Out of the Way
items.background: This appears to be a short-form piece making a distinction between interfaces that reduce friction passively versus those actively designed to help users make progress toward a goal.
keyFindings: The core claim is that reducing cognitive load alone is insufficient — interfaces should orient users toward next actions, not just remove obstacles.
The piece distinguishes between 'don't make me think' as a passive goal versus forward momentum as an active design target.
items.implications: Thin on specifics given the snippet, and the article title is missing — treat with caution as a reference. The underlying distinction between friction-removal and goal-progression is worth considering in navigation and onboarding flows.

items.headline: EBT Card Lock UI Fails Users Who Need Clarity Most
items.background: Connect EBT is one of the primary apps used by SNAP recipients to manage their benefits. Card lock and unlock features are critical for fraud prevention, but poor UX can leave vulnerable users confused about whether their card is active and where it will work.
keyFindings: The existing card lock/unlock interface fails to clearly communicate the scope of the lock — users can't easily tell which transaction types or merchant categories are affected.
The redesign proposal focuses on plain-language state indicators and contextual explanations of when and where the card will function.
The piece identifies that unclear status states are a specific failure mode — users couldn't tell if the card was locked or unlocked at a glance.
items.implications: A concrete case study for anyone designing access-control or account-state UIs for users with low digital literacy or high-stakes needs. The specific failure mode — ambiguous toggle states without scope explanation — applies broadly to fintech and benefits products.

items.headline: Research Paper Asks How Service Design Works Without Screens
items.background: As AI agents begin handling multi-step tasks autonomously — booking, purchasing, troubleshooting — the assumption that service design centers on screen-based interfaces is increasingly challenged. Winjit's paper, launched at GFF 2026, attempts to address this gap.
keyFindings: The paper argues that agentic AI systems require service design frameworks that don't depend on visual UI as the primary touchpoint.
It proposes rethinking service blueprints and touchpoint maps for contexts where AI agents act on behalf of users without presenting interfaces.
The work was formally presented at GFF 2026, suggesting some institutional weight, though it originates from a technology vendor.
items.implications: Relevant for service designers and product strategists working on AI agent products or voice/ambient interfaces. Note that this comes from a vendor (Winjit), so treat the framing as a starting point for the conversation rather than independent research.

items.headline: Practical Guide to Starting a UX Career in Africa
items.background: UX design education and career resources are heavily skewed toward North American and European markets. Designers in African countries face different constraints around tooling access, portfolio expectations, and hiring pipelines.
keyFindings: The guide addresses region-specific challenges including limited access to paid tools like Figma's advanced tiers and sparse local UX job markets in some countries.
It outlines an entry path through community participation, open-source projects, and remote-first companies as primary hiring channels.
Covers which portfolio platforms and networking spaces are most active and relevant for African designers seeking local or global roles.
items.implications: Directly useful for junior designers in African markets or those mentoring them. Also worth noting for recruiters and hiring managers at remote-first companies — the guide signals where to find and engage emerging talent pools.
